name: Cozi Gold
subcategory: family organization, recipes and household inventory
tagline: Share a household calendar, lists, chores, and simple meal notes

tiers.name: Cozi Free
tiers.limits: Shared calendar, lists and recipes for the family; no numeric caps disclosed.

tiers.name: Cozi Gold
tiers.limits: Whole-family upgrade; no ads, mobile month view, calendar search, up to 3 reminders per event, change notifications, birthday tracker, shopping mode, premium support.
tiers.notes: Official page says $39 on web or in-app purchase; no monthly price published.

pricing.freeTierCaps: free plan exists with shared calendar/lists/recipes; no numeric caps disclosed.
pricing.billingTerms: annual on public page ($39/year); no monthly plan published
pricing.hiddenCosts: Gold applies to everyone in the family; free tier is ad-supported.

verdictSummary: The core loop is small enough for a capable coding agent to produce a useful local version in one sitting. For Cozi Gold, share a household calendar, lists, chores, and simple meal notes. The hard boundary is family adoption, mobile apps, reminders, sync, and years of household workflow polish, plus sync, integrations, and household adoption.
coreLoopDIY: Share a household calendar, lists, chores, and simple meal notes, print or share a simple plan, and keep the data portable and owner-controlled.
whatYouLose: family adoption, mobile apps, reminders, sync, and years of household workflow polish
ongoingBurden: multi-user conflicts, reminders, notifications, imports, barcode data, smart-home APIs, backups, and long-term maintenance
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Cozi Gold because household apps survive when every family member actually uses them and the data stays current across devices. The recurring cost buys multi-user conflicts, reminders, notifications, imports, barcode data, smart-home APIs, backups, and long-term maintenance, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Mealie
priorArt.desc: Active open-source recipe manager and meal planner for households.

alternatives.name: Cozi Free
alternatives.desc: The same shared calendar, lists, tasks, and recipes for $0; the ads and nicer controls stay upstairs.

alternatives.name: Family Tools Basic
alternatives.desc: Calendar, chores, and shared lists for twelve people; meal planning is exactly where the paywall starts.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Homechart
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Looks free and self-hosted; shared households still require a paid subscription.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Gold plan and a single-household organizer DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Cozi Gold in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, SQLite, Drizzle ORM, and a local-first PWA; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: share a household calendar, lists, chores, and simple meal notes, print or share a simple plan, and keep the data portable and owner-controlled.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create household members, shared lists, calendar items, recipes or inventory records, and assignments.
Provide fast mobile-first capture with large controls, offline queueing, and conflict-safe sync to one server.
Support recurring chores or events, reminders, completion history, and printable views.
Add CSV or JSON import and export plus photo attachments with clear size limits.
Allow private and shared items and make every change attributable and undoable.
Add backups, household export, member removal, and a simple invite code.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out retailer ordering and proprietary product catalogs.
Deliberately leave out broad smart-home integrations.
Deliberately leave out large public recipe libraries and polished native mobile clients.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
